idiomatic: At upper-origin year jiazi: civil new year jiazi new moon, winter solstice at midnight; sun, moon, and five planets at the start of Void; yin-yang and slow-fast sequences also begin here.

literal: In the third year of Liang Emperor Wu's Tianjian reign, Chongzhi's son Heng submitted a memorial discussing the errors of He Chengtian's calendar, that it could not be used.
idiomatic: Liang Tianjian year 3: Zu Chongzhi's son Heng memorialized that He Chengtian's calendar was erroneous and unusable.

literal: In the first month of the ninth year, an edict ordered the Jiazi Epoch Calendar Chongzhi had made to be used to issue the new moon.
idiomatic: In year 9, month 1, an edict adopted Zu Chongzhi's Jiazi Epoch Calendar for issuing the new moon.

literal: Chen followed Liang and also used Chongzhi's calendar.
idiomatic: Chen continued Liang practice and used Chongzhi's calendar.

literal: Reaching Liao, Emperor Shengzong took the new calendar Jia Jun presented and, keeping the old Song title Great Brightness, put it into use.
idiomatic: Under Liao, Emperor Shengzong adopted Jia Jun's new calendar while retaining the Song name Great Brightness.

literal: Jin called it the Revised Great Brightness Calendar.
idiomatic: Jin titled it the Revised Great Brightness Calendar.

literal: Transmitted to the Yuan it was also called the Revised Great Brightness Calendar.
idiomatic: In the Yuan it was likewise the Revised Great Brightness Calendar.

literal: When the Season-Granting Calendar was adopted, a separate Directorate of Astronomy was established to preserve study; each jiazi year at winter solstice its methods were revised.
idiomatic: After the Season-Granting Calendar replaced it, a Directorate of Astronomy kept the old methods, revised at each jiazi winter solstice.

literal: The book was kept in the Imperial Astronomical Archive; access was forbidden.
idiomatic: The text remained in the Grand Astrologer's archive, barred from circulation.
